newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli negotiator says PLO peace concerns "real".
newsitem.headline: Israeli negotiator says PLO peace concerns "real".

text.p: Israel's chief negotiator with the Palestinians said on Thursday he thought their concerns about the continuation of the peace process were valid.

"They have concerns, and I say they are real concerns... regarding the continuation of the peace process, the redeployment not only in Hebron, continuation of the redeployment," Dan Shomron told Israel Radio.

"There are parts of the agreement some of which were to have been implemented by this past September 7," Shomron said, referring to a year-old agreement signed by Israel's previous government to hand much of the West Bank to Palestinian rule.
The former Israeli army chief of staff did not elaborate on why he thought the Palestinian concerns valid.
Shomron is heading the Israeli side to talks on implementing an Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron, which under the year-old deal should have occurred in March.
Hebron, revered by both Moslems and Jews as the burial place of Abraham, has become the symbol that divides them and has long been a flashpoint of violence.

Shomron said talks on Hebron were snagged mainly because the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) was trying to put assurances that the further redeployments would be carried out into the Hebron protocol.

"The issue of Hebron in the eyes of the Palestinians is not an issue on its own. They see the entire process and want, via the conclusion of the protocol on Hebron, to also put in issues that are connected to the entire process and this causes great difficulty in concluding," Shomron said.
But Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, in the Nablus West Bank self-rule enclave on Thursday, again blamed Israel for holding up the Hebron deal.
"They are intentionally delaying this agreement. Look, in the last days just one meeting was held," Arafat told reporters.
Palestinian negotiator Hassan Asfour, who attended a meeting with Shomron on Wednesday, said there was no progress.
On Wednesday, Arafat appealed to re-elected U.S. President Bill Clinton for a "quick push" to get Middle East peacemaking back on track.
But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Arabs not to expect a second-term Clinton, despite being unfettered by re-election concerns, to pressure Israel into making concessions.

U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross left the region on October 29 after failing to broker a Hebron deal in three weeks of talks. The U.S. Consul-General to Arab East Jerusalem Edward Abington said earlier this week that the sides were still too far apart on a Hebron deal to warrant Ross's return.

Under the deal signed by Israel's previous government with the PLO, Israel was to hand six West Bank towns to Palestinian rule and partially withdraw from Hebron, the only one of the seven with Jews living inside it -- 400 amid 100,000 Palestinians. A handover of rural areas was to begin after the Hebron redeployment.
The six towns were handed over in late 1995, before Israel's May 1996 elections in which the right-wing Netanyahu ousted the previous centre-left government.

Palestinians fear that Netanyahu, who opposes the principle of trading occupied Arab land for peace which was the basis of negotiations with the previous Israeli government, wants to foil the peace deals based on the principle.
